transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

Hi. Well, I'm here because I just... I can't stop focusing on my face. I'm a high school teacher, and whenever I see myself on our recorded lesson videos, all I can see is this crooked, swollen-looking side of my face. 

It's really getting to me. Once I notice it, I just feel like the students, the parents, the rest of the staff... I feel like they must all be staring right at it instead of actually listening to anything I'm saying.
Have family, friends, or colleagues ever noticed or mentioned that your face looks crooked or swollen?

No, um... no one has actually ever said anything to me about it. Not my family, or any of the other teachers. 

I mean, I haven't heard them mention it. I kind of just assume they're being polite and trying not to point it out, because it's so incredibly obvious to me. But directly to my face? No, they haven't.
Do you find yourself spending a significant amount of time checking your face in mirrors, trying to cover it up, or fixing it throughout the day?

Yeah, I do. It takes up a lot of my time, actually. Um, especially with work. 

Before I post a recorded lesson or join a parent conference, I just... I keep changing the camera angle. I'll replay the video clips over and over to check how I look, or I'll catch myself covering parts of my face with my hand while I'm on screen. And with the recorded lessons, I end up re-recording the whole thing so many times because I can't stand seeing it. It gets to the point where I... I actually miss my prep work, and I end up being late with my classes.
Could you consider the possibility that your face might not be as noticeably crooked or swollen as you feel it is, or are you completely convinced it truly looks that way?

I mean... I hear what you're saying, but I just can't see it any other way. When I look at the screen or in the mirror, it's just right there. It's so clear to me. I guess part of my brain knows that since no one else has brought it up, maybe it isn't as huge as I think it is, but... I'm pretty convinced it really looks that way. It's just hard to believe otherwise when I see it so clearly myself.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F22 as the patient demonstrates some insight (acknowledging that others haven't noticed and that it might not be as huge as perceived), confirming non-delusional dysmorphophobia classified under F45.2.
